You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: In-depth Analysis of Rubin Ultra Downgrade Rumors: How Much Less HBM4E Demand, and Will DRAM Price Increases and Memory Stock Revaluation Reverse?

TEXT:
TL;DR
1. SemiAnalysis research from July 29 indicates that the mainstream Ultra SKU adopts HBM4 8-Hi, 192GB, approximately 21TB/s and 1,800W Max-Q, with peak theoretical FLOPs equal to Rubin, with the main upgrade shifting to the 576-GPU scale-up domain; Nvidia has so far only confirmed the current Rubin’s 288GB HBM4, 12-Hi and 22TB/s, as well as Ultra NVL576’s 8×72-GPU topology, and has not yet confirmed the above mentioned Ultra specs.
2. Two benchmarks for capacity impact: relative to the current Rubin’s 288GB, 192GB is a 33.3% drop, but a 50% increase in GPU count can offset it; compared to the previous 2-die Ultra HBM4E 12-Hi at 384GB, it is a 50% drop, and doubling GPU count is needed to offset. The earliest 4-die 1,024GB solution simultaneously changed the number of dies, power consumption, and system definition; the 81.25% physical capacity gap cannot be directly equated to a downward revision in industry demand.
3. Based on each GPU having 192GB and the official 576-GPU domain estimate, NVL576 contains 110.592TB of HBM, which is 5.33 times Rubin NVL72. Larger expansion domains do not prove actual output volume, but indicate that demand is shifting from “single GPU high capacity” to “more low-power GPUs”; compared to the 384GB old Ultra solution, system or GPU counts must increase by 100% to maintain the same bit demand.
4. There is still little direct impact on 2026 prices. Ultra targets 2027, with Rubin HBM4, AI ASIC, and server DRAM demand realized in 2026. Inventories are low among the three major manufacturers, contract coverage is rising, and HBM4 is ramping up. The negatives are concentrated in 2027 when mainstream Ultra switches from HBM4E back to HBM4, affecting the incremental increase in high-layer products, per-GB premium, and supplier mix.
5. The impact on overall DRAM is much smaller than on the HBM4E mix. If Ultra originally accounted for 20% of 2027 HBM bit demand, and the same architecture drops from 384GB to 192GB, total industry HBM bit demand is revised down about 10%, which translates to about 1.3% of all DRAM bit demand, or about 3% of theoretical DRAM wafer input. This will flatten price increase slopes, but it is not enough to prove oversupply on its own.
6. As of July 31, Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung Electronics have retreated 32.2%, 41.1%, and 27.6% from their year-to-date high closes, but are still up 188.4%, 163.9%, and 118.9% year-to-date, respectively. The SemiAnalysis scenario is least favorable for SK Hynix’s long-term HBM4E scarcity premium, with Micron in the middle, while Samsung is more resilient due to its more diversified business and lower 8-Hi entry barriers; this only ranks sensitivity, not current profitability reversals.
To avoid losing touch, feel free to follow the backup account, where updates are posted daily.
Table of Contents Join Knowledge Planet to view the full original report and reference research report.
I. Official Parameters & Unverified Fields
II. Three Layers of HBM Demand Impact Calculation
III. Why HBM and DRAM Prices Won’t Immediately Reverse in 2026
IV. In 2027, HBM4E Premium and Product Mix Are Most Impacted
V. Remaining Sections
SemiAnalysis says Rubin Ultra’s mainstream solution has been reduced to HBM4 8-Hi, 192GB, and 1,800W Max-Q. If this supply chain scenario holds, the impact will mainly fall on the 2027 HBM4E product mix and memory stock valuations, not on 2026 DRAM price trends.
I. Official Parameters & Unverified Fields
Nvidia’s Rubin architecture, released July 21, shows that a single Rubin GPU is composed of two compute dies, offering up to 50 PF NVFP4 inference performance, 35 PF NVFP4 training performance, 288GB HBM4, 12-Hi stack, and 22TB/s bandwidth. 72 GPUs in an NVL72 system totals about 20.7TB HBM. Nvidia’s public info on Ultra still stops at system topology: Rubin Ultra NVL576 consists of 8 MGX NVL racks, each with 72 Ultra GPUs, forming a 576-GPU NVLink domain.
SemiAnalysis’ July 29 supply chain research further gives a mainstream Ultra scenario: 2 compute dies, HBM4, 8 groups of 8-Hi, 192GB, about 21TB/s, and 1,800W Max-Q, with peak theoretical FLOPs matching Rubin; there may also be 2,600—2,800W Max-P, and a 1,200W version for lower compute workloads like token decode. Their comparison table uses 35 PF, matching Nvidia’s official 35 PF NVFP4 training spec—this cannot be directly compared with the 50 PF sparse inference number. Info on 192GB, power tiers, and NPO rack interconnect has yet to appear in Nvidia’s official Ultra datasheet.
The core change in the roadmap is 1,024GB→768GB→384GB→192GB , along with 4-die cancellation, HBM4E reverting to HBM4, and power dropping. The original chart has arithmetic labeling ambiguities for HBM stack count and capacity in intermediate stages, so stack count is not used for demand calculation; mainstream capacity, HBM generation, die count, and power match the narrative described here.
[...]
110.592TB is the unofficial estimate based on Nvidia’s current “576 Ultra GPUs” and 192GB per GPU. If SemiAnalysis’s 192GB actually refers to physical package of two dies, and 576 counts compute dies, total capacity would be 55.296TB; this interpretation does not match Nvidia’s current official specs and is only a secondary boundary. The earliest 4-die system’s 144 packages and the current 576 GPUs use different denominators, so the drop from 147.456TB to 110.592TB can’t be directly plugged into industry demand models.
[...]
If only compared with current Rubin 288GB, results at 20% weight are milder: HBM total demand drops 6.7%, all DRAM bit demand falls 0.9%, theoretical wafer input releases 2%. Both sets of results do not deduct for increased GPU deployments, Google TPU/AI ASIC demand, AMD platforms, Max-P SKUs, supplier yields, locked contracts, or wafer reallocations. The importance of Ultra spec changes to the HBM4E product mix is far greater than to overall DRAM impact; the latter will not mechanically fall by double digits as a result.
[...]
First, timing mismatch. Ultra targets 2027, and 2026 production is driven by Rubin HBM4 and AI ASIC. In its 2Q26 earnings, SK Hynix says HBM4 has started volume shipments and signed long-term agreements with around 10 key customers; Micron in its fiscal 2026 Q3 says HBM4 is now shipping in large quantities to leading customers, with HBM4E expected to enter mass production in 2027, and long-term strategic agreements improving visibility. 2027 SKUs not yet on Nvidia’s official datasheet will not affect already certified, in-process, and delivered 2026 products.
[...]
Third, SemiAnalysis’s downgrade motivation itself points to supply tightness, not demand destruction. Their view is that Nvidia must allocate limited HBM to more GPUs, rebalancing between relatively looser TSMC frontend and tighter HBM supply, while offsetting 2027 price hikes with lower HBM and power supply BOM. If so, per-GPU capacity reduction actually proves HBM and datacenter power remain bottlenecks. The degree to which 1,800W Max-Q increases deployability will determine whether per-GPU cuts translate to system-wide volume drops.
[...]
Fourth, HBM is not solely a Nvidia story. TrendForce sees 2026 HBM growth mainly from AI ASICs, with 2027 driven by both Rubin Ultra and AI ASIC. Even if Ultra’s per-card capacity decreases, TPUs and other dedicated accelerators, AMD platforms, Max-P versions, and other customers may partially fill the gap. Changes in a single Nvidia mainstream SKU cannot be taken as representing the entire HBM industry demand.
